name: Lengthened partials / stretch training
lead: Lengthened partials are repetitions performed only in the stretched portion of an exercise, such as the bottom half of a curl, fly or pulldown, rather than through the full range of motion. Lifters use them to place the most tension on a muscle when it is at its longest, with the aim of building more muscle, for example wider shoulders, a thicker upper chest or fuller arms, which many pursue as part of a stronger physique [1][2].

The Wikipedia hypertrophy article reports that full range of motion, particularly at elongated muscle lengths, is described as enhancing growth more than partial range, and that partial-range training at long lengths is also said to promote hypertrophy, possibly through muscle damage [1]. In lifting communities the technique is often described alongside a broader shift toward emphasising the stretched position of each exercise [2][3].

A 2025 randomized within-participant trial in 30 resistance-trained adults compared lengthened partials with full-range repetitions over eight weeks of upper-body training and reported similar gains in elbow flexor and extensor thickness and lat pulldown 10-rep max between the two conditions [2][6].

angle.text: Lifters add lengthened partials to build muscle in areas such as delts, chest and triceps. The technique works through training volume and tension at long muscle lengths rather than through any change to the body outside the gym.

paras: Lifters either finish a set with extra partial reps in the lengthened range or build whole sets from them. Proponents link the approach to the idea that muscles grow well when loaded at long lengths [1]. Exercises that lend themselves to it include leg extensions, curls, flies and pulldowns; T Nation members describe adding lengthened partials to leg extensions and to a physique program aimed at wider delts, a thicker upper chest and fuller triceps [4][5].

The technique sits within a wider vocabulary of partial repetitions. A T Nation poster, for instance, notes that bands make the shortened position harder and add little resistance in the lengthened position, which they argue is the wrong way round for hypertrophy [8]. Others recount older partial-rep ideas, such as lengthening the range of movement every few workouts until full range is reached [9].

Reviews of muscle hypertrophy describe mechanical tension as the currently accepted driver of growth and note that exercise at long muscle lengths is described as beneficial [1]. Proponents argue that the stretched position is where muscle fibres experience high tension and where many exercises are easiest, so partial reps there let lifters keep loading a muscle after full-range reps become hard [1][5]. The idea is separate from stretching as a flexibility habit: a 2025 Delphi consensus of 20 research experts agreed that stretch training itself does not contribute substantively to muscle growth, while it does improve range of motion [10].

A 2026 review in Sports Medicine International Open by Pedrosa, Pereira and Kassiano proposes that muscle length is necessary but not sufficient: the largest gains, in their model, come when a muscle is loaded at a long length and external torque is also high in that position.[11] Candidate mechanisms the review discusses include passive tension from elastic structures such as titin contributing to mechanosensing, greater muscle swelling at long lengths, and possibly greater motor unit recruitment, and the authors say these remain hypotheses.[11] They also note that most included studies used untrained participants and ran 5 to 15 weeks, and that muscles such as the pectorals and lats have not been studied.[11]

Several trials outside the lengthened-partial design inform the idea. In a 12-week study of untrained young women described in the 2026 review, knee extension through an initial (long-length) range produced larger rectus femoris growth at a site 70 percent along the thigh than full range (30.2 versus 17.7 percent), and much more than training only the shortened range (1.2 percent).[11] The same review reports that full range outperformed shortened-range training in several studies, while initial and full range often produced similar or greater growth, with some studies finding no difference.[11]

Exercise-selection studies by Maeo and colleagues compared movements that stretch a muscle more with those that stretch it less. In 12 weeks of triceps training, overhead extensions (elbow extension with the arm overhead, lengthening the long head) produced greater whole-triceps growth than the neutral-arm version (19.9 versus 13.9 percent), and seated leg curls produced greater hamstring growth than prone curls (14.1 versus 9.3 percent), as summarised in the review.[11] These studies compare exercise variants rather than lengthened partials, and the authors of the review caution that the results involve mostly untrained participants and short durations.[11]
Together with the 2025 trained-lifter trial, this body of work is why many lifters emphasise stretched positions in exercise choice, whether or not they use partial repetitions.[2][11]

In the 2025 PeerJ trial, 30 resistance-trained participants trained each arm with a different range of motion, lengthened partials or full range, for eight weeks. Training involved two sessions a week with four exercises per session and four sets per exercise; muscle thickness of the elbow flexors and extensors was measured by ultrasonography at 45 and 55 percent of humeral length, and lat pulldown 10-rep max was tested [2][6].

Gains in muscle thickness and 10-rep max were similar, with Bayes factors from 0.16 to 0.3 giving moderate support for no difference between conditions. The authors concluded that trainees seeking size should likely emphasise the stretched position, whether through full range or lengthened partials [2][6].

A systematic review of resistance training and range of motion found that lifting can improve flexibility, and a 2023 meta-analysis of 55 studies compared resistance training with stretch training for that outcome [7].

Lifters who use stretch-focused training typically do so to build visible size in specific areas: overhead triceps work for arm thickness, incline or stretch-position flies for the upper chest, lateral-raise variants for shoulder width, and leg extensions for the quadriceps. Because proportions and shoulder-to-waist ratio shape how a physique looks, programs that aim to maximise growth per set are of interest to people building an aesthetic physique.[5][11]

The technique is commonly described as a way to extend a set: once full-range reps become difficult, the lifter continues with partial reps in the stretched range. Others build entire sets from the lower half of the movement.[1][2]

On T Nation the technique is discussed both enthusiastically and sceptically. One poster calls lengthened partials the latest science-based training fad, while others report using them in their own logs, including for leg extensions and for physique goals [3][4][5].

One randomized trial directly compares lengthened partials with full-range training in trained participants and found similar muscle thickness and strength-endurance gains [2][6]. Reviews of resistance training and stretching examine range-of-motion improvements more broadly [7][10].

A 2022 trial of 12 weeks of knee-extension training in young women, reported in the 2026 review, compared initial-range, full-range and final-range training and found larger growth in some quadriceps regions with the long-length range.[11] This trial and the exercise-selection studies of Maeo and colleagues involved mostly untrained participants and are summarised in the review rather than in this article's primary sources.[11]

timeline.event: Trial of knee-extension training at long, full and short ranges in untrained young women published (Pedrosa and colleagues).[11]
A PeerJ randomized trial compares lengthened partials with full range of motion in 30 trained lifters [2].
A Delphi consensus of 20 experts publishes recommendations on stretching, including its effect on muscle growth [10].

lore.intro: Lengthened partials spread through lifting communities as research on training at long muscle lengths became popular; T Nation threads show lifters trying them and others questioning the trend.[3][4][5]

claims.claim: Training the stretched position grows more muscle
claims.believers: Lifters say overloading the lengthened position is working for their delts, upper chest and triceps.[5]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes long-muscle-length exercise as beneficial for hypertrophy, while a 2025 trial in trained lifters found lengthened partials and full range gave similar gains.[1][2]

claims.claim: Lengthened partials are a passing fad
claims.believers: One T Nation poster describes them as the latest science-based training fad.[3]
claims.experts: Researchers have published a controlled comparison showing similar adaptations to full range training.[2]

claims.claim: Reps in the stretched position are especially useful for physique goals such as wider delts and thicker chest.
claims.believers: A lifter on T Nation says lengthened partials from the stretched position seem to be working for widening the delts, thickening the upper chest and improving the triceps [5].
claims.experts: The 2025 trial found muscle thickness gains in the arms were similar for lengthened partials and full range, with authors advising emphasis on the stretched position [2][6].

claims.believers: Some lifters treat stretch-position loading as a way to add size beyond normal training [1].
claims.experts: A Delphi consensus of 20 experts agreed that stretch training does not contribute substantively to muscle growth [10].

card.summary: Overloading only the stretched part of a rep; plausible in hypertrophy theory, thinly documented here.
card.note: Thin sources; no dedicated trials summarised.

quick.overview:
Lengthened partials are repetitions done only in the stretched portion of a lift. Lifters use them to load muscles at long lengths.

Hypertrophy overviews describe training at long muscle lengths as beneficial, but no dedicated trials were summarised here.
quick.mechanism: The technique aims to keep mechanical tension high while the muscle is elongated, which proponents link to growth.
quick.risks: Heavy loading in stretched positions can stress joints and connective tissue, as with other resistance training. No technique-specific harm data were identified.
